summary: A traveller describes a broken statue left in the desert. The statue is of the once mighty ruler Ozymandias, who claims to be the “king of kings”. The ruler is incredibly arrogant and proud, conveying the hubris of powerful rulers. However, the fact that nothing is left of his empire shows how the power of humans will always vanish over time and nothing can prevent it.
context: Shelley was a Romantic poet who believed in the supreme power of nature. This is reflected in the poem because the statue has eroded and is being swallowed by the sand. Humanity is presented as weak and insignificant because our power always diminishes over time. He also conveys how leaders can abuse their power, giving the poem a political message that society should avoid allowing some people to hold too much power over others.

summary: The speaker describes wandering through the streets of London and seeing the terrible squalor that the poor must endure. It explores the suffering and lack of freedom that people in society have. The poem conveys how there is a rigid divide in society between the rich and poor, even suggesting that the poor are psychologically controlled by the ruling class.
context: Blake was a Romantic poet who believed that the Industrial Era was stripping individuals of their freedoms. He therefore wrote this poem to encourage society to realise the way that they are being oppressed by those in power. The poem reveals that often those in power have brainwashed the working-class so they do not question or reject the status quo. People have simply become objects and commodities in the eyes of the ruling class.
form_notes: Regular rhyme scheme ABAB (can suggest control, strength, repetition, or being trapped).

summary: The speaker steals a boat and rows onto a lake. At the beginning, the speaker seems overconfident and reckless, representing how humanity often have a similar attitude, believing they are more powerful than they are. However, the speaker sees a mountain and suddenly realises how weak he is in comparison to the supreme power of nature. He rows back to shore and is forever changed by his experience, knowing that he is nothing compared to the omnipotence of nature.
context: Wordsworth was a Romantic poet who believed that nature held supreme power and that humanity was weak and insignificant in comparison. He wrote his poetry as a reaction to the Industrial Revolution, which saw society prioritise human engineering and industry over nature. Wordsworth reflects this idea in the poem by showing the arrogant and reckless attitude of humanity through the speaker, emphasising their foolish disregard of nature. This poem is also inspired by Wordsworth’s own experiences, emphasising how this realisation was an important life lesson he learned when growing up.
form_notes: An extract from a long autobiographical epic poem; written in iambic pentameter.

summary: The speaker is a wealthy and powerful Duke who is showing a messenger round his manor. As he shows his guest around, he boasts about all the rich possessions he has, including a painting of his dead wife. He describes his dead wife to the guest, revealing his paranoid worries that she may have had affairs with other men. He even implies that he may have ordered his wife to be killed. This poem conveys the control that men often try to assert over women in a patriarchal society.
context: Browning was writing during the Victorian Era, when society held strict patriarchal values. This poem reflects this idea by conveying the way that women are often regarded as the property of their husbands. Moreover, the way the poem is written only from the perspective of the Duke highlights how women are often stripped of their voice and are rendered powerless by society. Despite seeming powerful, Browning also suggests that the Duke is incredibly paranoid and fears the power of his wife, conveying how fragile his sense of masculinity is too.
title_analysis: “My” (possessive pronoun) shows the Duke’s ownership; “last” suggests she was one of several wives and will be replaced; “Duchess” reduces her to her status. She is never given a name or a voice.

poem: The Charge of the Light Brigade
summary: About the Battle of Balaclava in the Crimean War, between Britain (and allies) and Russia. The Light Brigade, British cavalry on horses with light weapons such as swords, were told to charge into a valley at the Russian enemy. The command was wrong, and they charged into a valley where Russians were waiting with guns and cannons, so many British soldiers were needlessly killed.
context: Tennyson did not fight in the Crimean War. The Crimean War is often considered the first media war: newspapers carried eye-witness reports. The Times described how 600 British men were killed because of a “hideous blunder”. Incensed by the futile loss of life, Tennyson was inspired by the newspaper report to write the poem.
form_notes: Ballad; dactylic dimeter (6 syllables: one stressed, two unstressed), with a galloping rhythm that changes as the horses fall and the army realises its mistake.

summary: Describes the collective experiences of soldiers in the trenches during WW1. The poem conveys the terrible hardships and suffering they must endure. However, rather than present the enemy as the opposing army, Owen suggests that their real enemy are the conditions they face: the boredom, the weather, and the psychological trauma they experience. It conveys the cruel power of nature that tortures them both physically and mentally.
context: Owen was a soldier during WW1 and experienced first-hand the terrible conditions of the trenches. He suffered from shell-shock and wrote the poem to reveal the reality of war and to “expose” what life was really like for soldiers. His poem contradicts the traditional view of war created by propaganda that had made young men believe that fighting for your country was noble and honourable. In reality, the soldiers were living in squalor and dying in undignified ways for a futile cause. Owen died on 4 November 1918, one week before the war ended.
title_analysis: Soldiers are exposed to the weather and to danger; Owen wants to expose the truth about war to the reader; and he exposes the troubled thoughts of the soldiers’ psychological state. (The lesson sets this out as a mind-map for students to complete; the wording here follows the lesson’s four prompts and the revision guide.)

summary: Describes an aggressive and destructive storm attacking an island. The people who live on the island experience this frequently, so they prepare themselves to constantly suffer the attacks. Despite their fear, they seem to be resilient. The poet uses an extended metaphor throughout the poem: the storm is actually a metaphor for the Troubles in Ireland. The poem conveys the destruction that the Troubles inflicted upon Ireland and the way that the Irish people showed their resilience in enduring it.
context: Heaney has Irish heritage and saw first-hand the devastating impact of the Troubles on the Irish people. He uses this poem to convey the terrible damage that is repeatedly inflicted by the conflict, how the attacks disrupted ordinary domestic life and could strike at any time without warning, and the strong spirit of the Irish people who stayed resilient during this time. The Troubles were a period of conflict in Ireland during the 1970s, 80s and 90s between Catholic (wanting independence) and Protestant (wanting to stay part of the UK) sides.

summary: About a soldier in WW1 who has been told to suddenly charge at the enemy. As he runs desperately across the battlefield, he questions why he is there. He is consumed by fear.
context: Hughes did not fight in WW1 but was inspired by the tragic stories of the soldiers. WW1 propaganda promised young men they would be respected heroes, or pressured them into believing they were cowards for not signing up; in reality, soldiers lived in terrible conditions in the trenches, treated like cannon-fodder.

summary: The speaker is a war veteran describing a memory from when he was a soldier. He describes how on one occasion he shot and killed a looter. He is traumatised by the experience and feels incredible guilt. Even when he returns home he is consumed by his PTSD.
context: Armitage wrote the poem for a documentary called ‘The Not Dead’, in which war veterans explained how their experiences in conflict had affected their lives, including how difficult it was to readjust to life after returning home.
form_notes: Colloquial language; starts in media res (“On another occasion…”); the volta is “End of story, except not really.”; the title can mean human remains, what remains of the soldier’s mind, or what lingers on.
title_analysis: “Remains” can mean human remains (what is physically left of a dead body); it can refer to what remains of the soldier’s mind; and it also means something that lasts, endures or lingers on.

summary: The speaker is a mother whose son was killed in war. She remembers the beautiful and tender memories of him growing up. However, now these memories are painful for her because she is consumed by grief. She is haunted by the thought of how he died.
form_notes: Dramatic monologue (the mother speaks to her son); two semantic fields: war and pain (bandaged, spasms, blockade, graze, reinforcements) and fabric and clothing (scarf, shirt, felt, skirting, tucks, darts, pleats, coat, gloves, stitch).

summary: The speaker is a photojournalist who has visited many conflict zones to capture the impact of war. The poem describes how, when he returns safely home and is in his darkroom, he remembers the traumatic things he witnessed.
context: The poem was written in the 1980s.
form_notes: Extended metaphor of the darkroom as a church; controlled, regular rhyme scheme ABBCDD, with caesura and enjambment disrupting the rhythm.

summary: Describes how paper is both fragile and valuable. Dharker uses paper as an extended metaphor for human life.
context: The poet is a proud Muslim; her love of God guides her.
form_notes: Extended metaphor; semantic fields of hard stone (buildings, monoliths…) and light (luminous…).
title_analysis: “Tissue” is fragile, which represents human life; paper is important; tissue lets light through; and people forget how valuable paper is. Tissue also links to human flesh and skin.

summary: The speaker is a refugee who has fled her country because it has become a dangerous place, destroyed by war and ruled by cruel dictators. She sees her homeland through rose-tinted glasses and even though it was a violent place, she remembers it positively and feels love for her home. She dreams of going back, even though it is still not safe for her to return.
context: Rumens is not a refugee. However, she was inspired by the stories of refugees and wanted to write this poem to give them a voice because they are often ignored and not listened to by society. The home country of the speaker is not revealed. This ambiguity gives the poem a timeless relevance and allows readers from across the world to relate to the character in the poem.
form_notes: Juxtaposition of positive and negative connotations (e.g. sunlight and November).

summary: The speaker describes the way he was given an education that focused on white-British history, and his education failed to teach him about his true heritage or about black history. The poem conveys the way that the British Empire holds power over the countries it has colonised. It also shows the way they use education as a method of control. At the end of the poem, the speaker describes how he plans to carve out his identity, showing how he intends to embrace his true identity by learning about his ancestors and important black figures from history.
context: Agard was inspired to write the poem when he read in a school textbook that West Indian history began with the arrival of Christopher Columbus in 1492. He was outraged because this ignored the history of the native people who lived there before the coloniser, Columbus, arrived. The poem explores how education can be used to try to erase the culture, history and identity of colonised countries. Agard wants people to embrace their own history as a means of embracing their identity. The poem names Toussaint L’Ouverture, Nanny de Maroon and Mary Seacole.

summary: About a Japanese kamikaze pilot in WW2. As he flies over the sea, he decides to turn his plane around and return home. He spends the rest of his life being considered a coward and is shunned by his family and community.
context: Garland did not fight in WW2 but was inspired by the tragic stories of the kamikaze pilots. In WW2, Japan recruited young men to crash their planes into the enemy; many agreed because they had been indoctrinated to worship the Emperor as a living god and to see self-sacrifice as honourable.
form_notes: Starts in third person limited; half-way through, the perspective changes to first person (in italics): the pilot’s daughter speaking to her children about their grandfather.
